---
title: "Quiz: reconstruction as a linear system"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $\mathbf x$: pixel values, $\mathbf b$: measured ray sums, $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$.

---

**Q1.** What does row $i$ of $A$ contain, and why is $A$ sparse?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The weights with which ray $i$ sums the pixels: non-zero only for the pixels the ray passes through (path length or interpolation weights). A ray crosses a few hundred of the tens of thousands of pixels, so almost all entries are 0.
:::

---

**Q2.** Two different images give exactly the same data. What does that say about $A$, and what is their difference?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$A$ has a non-trivial **null space** (its rank is less than the number of pixels), and the difference of the two images lies in it: $A(\mathbf x_1 - \mathbf x_2) = 0$. The scan cannot see that pattern; more (or different) rays are needed.
:::

---

**Q3.** What is $A^\top\mathbf b$ in tomography terms, and why is it not the reconstruction?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Back-projection: each measurement is added back to the pixels of its ray with the same weights. It is not an inverse: $A^\top A \ne I$, so the result is blurred (the $1/r$ halo) and on the wrong scale.
:::

---

**Q4.** Describe one ART step in words.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One ray, its error, its pixels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Take one ray. Compute its error: measured value minus the current sum along the ray. Change the image as little as possible so that the ray is right: distribute the error over the ray's pixels in proportion to their weights (evenly, for equal weights), times the relaxation $\omega$. Move on to the next ray.
:::

---

**Q5.** ART is used with two very similar rays (neighbouring angles, almost the same pixels). Why is it slow?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Their equations are nearly parallel hyperplanes. Projecting from one to the other moves almost along both, so each step makes little progress towards their intersection: the zig-zag is long and narrow. Ordering the rays so that consecutive ones are very different (spread-out angles) helps.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why is the first SIRT step from a zero image a blurred image?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
From $\mathbf x = 0$ every ray's error is its measured value. SIRT back-projects all errors and averages: that is a normalised back-projection, $W_cA^\top W_r\mathbf b$, which has the halo of plain back-projection. The following steps correct it.
:::

---

**Q7.** In an iterative reconstruction of noisy data, the residual $\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf b\|$ keeps decreasing, but the images get noisier after some iterations. Why, and what can you do?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Semi-convergence: early iterations recover the well-measured, strong components of the image; later ones fit the weakly measured components, which are dominated by noise. A smaller residual then means fitting the noise. Stop early, or add a prior (e.g. TV) that penalises noise-like images.
:::

---

**Q8.** Name two priors used in tomography and what each assumes about the object.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Non-negativity**: attenuation (or tracer concentration) cannot be negative; clip negative values. **Total variation**: the object is mostly piecewise constant with sharp edges; penalise the sum of gradient magnitudes. Both remove streaks and noise when views are few, at the price of texture (TV) when the assumption is wrong.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Why does ART started from $\mathbf x = 0$ return the minimum-norm solution of a consistent system?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every update adds a multiple of a row $\mathbf a_i$, so the iterates stay in the row space of $A$, which is orthogonal to the null space. The limit is the solution with no null-space component; any other solution adds an orthogonal null-space vector and is longer (Pythagoras).
:::

---

**Q10.** *(math)* Write the TV-regularised reconstruction problem and name its two terms.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\hat{\mathbf x} = \arg\min_{\mathbf x \ge 0}\ \tfrac12\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf b\|^2 + \lambda\sum_p\|\nabla x_p\|$. The first term is the data term (agree with the measurements), the second the prior (be piecewise constant), weighted by $\lambda$, the same "data + λ · prior" form as the segmentation energies.
:::
